1987-01-03.title: John Lewis begins service in the U.S. House
paragraphs: John Lewis began his first term representing Georgia’s Fifth District on January 3, 1987. By then he had spent decades organizing for civil rights: he joined the Nashville sit-ins and Freedom Rides, chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and was beaten on the Edmund Pettus Bridge during the 1965 Selma march.

Congress followed Lewis’s service on Atlanta’s city council and his work with the national voter education effort. In the House he became a long-serving advocate for voting rights, drawing on the movement’s direct-action tradition and repeatedly bringing colleagues to Selma to remember the struggle behind federal protections.

1969-01-06.title: Ludie Clay Andrews dies after a life in nursing
paragraphs: Ludie Clay Andrews died on January 6, 1969, from injuries caused by a house fire. A graduate of Spelman’s nursing program, she helped organize Grady Hospital’s Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses in 1914 and later supervised nursing at MacVicar Hospital.

Andrews also challenged Georgia’s unequal licensing rules. When Black nurses were denied access to the state examination, she pressed for the same professional standard applied to white nurses rather than an exception for herself. Georgia Women of Achievement records that Black graduates of accredited programs gained access to the examination by 1920, a change with consequences for generations of nurses.

1994-01-10.title: Atlanta renames Houston Street for John Wesley Dobbs
paragraphs: On January 10, 1994, Atlanta renamed Houston Street John Wesley Dobbs Avenue. Mayor Maynard Jackson, Dobbs’s grandson, led the tribute to a civic organizer remembered as the “unofficial mayor” of Auburn Avenue, the commercial and cultural heart of Black Atlanta.

Dobbs had spent years building Black political power under segregation. With attorney A. T. Walden, he helped organize the Atlanta Negro Voters League, a bipartisan coalition that registered voters, screened candidates, and carried neighborhood demands to City Hall. The avenue name joined a public map to the organizing history that made Black votes harder for local politicians to ignore.

1929-01-15.title: Martin Luther King Jr. is born in Atlanta
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. was born on January 15, 1929, at 501 Auburn Avenue in Atlanta. His childhood unfolded in Sweet Auburn, a thriving Black neighborhood whose churches, businesses, and civic institutions stood within a city divided by segregation. At Ebenezer Baptist Church, his father and grandfather served as ministers, placing King in a family tradition of religious leadership.

King studied at Morehouse College, Crozer Theological Seminary, and Boston University before becoming pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery. The bus boycott there made him a national civil-rights leader. He later helped build the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and connected campaigns against segregation with economic justice and peace.

1969-01-15.title: Mourners gather at King’s South-View tomb on his birthday
paragraphs: On January 15, 1969, Martin Luther King Jr.’s birthday, mourners gathered at his tomb at South-View Cemetery. A National Museum of African American History and Culture photograph records the gravesite with an eternal flame and a wreath from Alpha Phi Alpha, the fraternity King had joined as a Morehouse student. The photograph captures a new public place of mourning less than a year after his assassination.

King’s body remained at South-View until January 1970, when it was moved to the grounds near Ebenezer Baptist Church. The brief South-View burial belongs to the immediate aftermath of his death, before the King Center complex and its permanent memorial took shape.

1983-01-15.title: Graham Jackson dies after a career in Atlanta music
paragraphs: Graham Washington Jackson Sr. died on January 15, 1983, after a career that moved between jazz, church music, theaters, and public life. After coming to Atlanta in 1924, he formed the Seminole Syncopators and performed on WSB radio; in 1928 he became music director at Booker T. Washington High School, then Atlanta’s public high school for Black students.

Jackson was also known for performances for Franklin D. Roosevelt, whom he met through Atlanta patrons. When Roosevelt’s body left Warm Springs in 1945, Jackson played the president’s favorite “Goin’ Home” on accordion. Ed Clark’s photograph of Jackson weeping as he played became one of the era’s enduring images of public grief.

1933-01-25.title: Dinah Watts Pace dies after building a home and school for children
paragraphs: Dinah Watts Pace died on January 25, 1933, after burns from a fire at her Covington home. Born enslaved near Athens, she completed Atlanta University’s normal course in 1883 and went to Covington to teach. There she encountered children with little access to schooling and care beyond what families could provide.

Pace took in two orphaned girls, and the work grew into the Covington Colored Orphans Home and school, later known as the Reed Home and School. She taught, housed children, and raised funds for the institution over decades. After her death, the school struggled to continue and closed in 1935.

1992-02-08.title: Bazoline E. Usher dies after decades in Atlanta education
paragraphs: Bazoline Estelle Usher died in Atlanta on February 8, 1992, aged 106. She had taught and led schools for decades, including fourteen years as principal of David T. Howard High School. She later supervised Atlanta’s Black schools while the city’s public education system remained segregated.

Usher also organized opportunities for Black girls outside school. In 1943 she recruited Black teachers and community volunteers to establish Girl Scout troops for African American girls in Atlanta. Her work linked classroom leadership to a wider effort to make civic, educational, and recreational programs accessible to Black children.

1886-02-20.title: Atlanta’s Black community moves to buy land for South-View
paragraphs: On February 20, 1886, the Atlanta Constitution reported that Black Atlantans were buying a new cemetery. As reproduced and discussed in D. L. Henderson’s history, the group had paid $600 toward a 25-acre tract on McDonough Road, priced at $3,500. The plan was already a community investment before South-View received its charter.

The six men who applied for the charter—Jacob McKinley, George W. Graham, Robert Grant, Charles H. Morgan, Albert Watts, and John Render—were Black business and civic leaders. Their project answered the humiliating treatment Black families faced at segregated burial grounds by creating an institution that Black Atlantans could own and govern.

1940-02-21.title: John Lewis is born near Troy, Alabama
paragraphs: John Robert Lewis was born on February 21, 1940, near Troy, Alabama, to sharecroppers. As a young man he heard Martin Luther King Jr. on the radio and began looking for a way to challenge the segregation that shaped Black life in the South.

Lewis joined the Nashville sit-ins and Freedom Rides, helped found the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and chaired it from 1963 to 1966. At twenty-three he spoke at the 1963 March on Washington. He later moved the work of voter registration and equal political participation into Atlanta public service and the U.S. House.

1903-02-22.title: Graham W. Jackson is born in Portsmouth, Virginia
paragraphs: Graham Washington Jackson was born in Portsmouth, Virginia, on February 22, 1903. He showed an early gift for piano and organ, then moved to Atlanta in 1924 to attend Morehouse College. Within months he had formed the Seminole Syncopators, an Atlanta jazz band that played on WSB radio and in local theaters.

Jackson built a career across Atlanta’s segregated musical world: he led music at Booker T. Washington High School, played church organ and the Fox Theatre’s Mighty Mo, and performed for presidents. His friendship with Franklin D. Roosevelt made Jackson’s 1945 accordion performance at Warm Springs an especially personal public tribute.

1908-02-22.title: Annie L. McPheeters is born in Floyd County
paragraphs: Annie Lou Watters was born in Berwin, Floyd County, Georgia, on February 22, 1908. After college and library training, she joined Atlanta’s Auburn Avenue branch, where she built a collection of books by and about Black people at a time when public institutions often excluded Black readers and history from their shelves.

McPheeters expanded that work through exhibits, reading programs, and campaigns for library desegregation. In 1966 she became Georgia State College’s first Black reference librarian. The collection and institutional knowledge she developed at Auburn Avenue helped lay the groundwork for the Auburn Avenue Research Library, which opened shortly before her death in 1994.

1965-03-07.title: Bloody Sunday: John Lewis and marchers are attacked in Selma
paragraphs: On March 7, 1965, John Lewis and Hosea Williams led hundreds of peaceful voting-rights marchers out of Selma toward Montgomery. At the Edmund Pettus Bridge, Alabama state troopers and deputized men ordered them to turn back, then struck the crowd with clubs and drove them with tear gas. Lewis suffered a fractured skull.

Television and newspaper coverage carried the violence far beyond Alabama. The marchers’ demand was the right to register and vote in a state where Black citizens faced systematic obstruction. Congress debated voting-rights legislation in the weeks that followed, and President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on August 6, 1965.

1886-03-18.title: A neighbor’s legal challenge interrupts South-View’s early burials
paragraphs: On March 18, 1886, the Atlanta Constitution reported that ten or twelve people had already been buried at the new South-View grounds. Adjoining landowner A. J. Harper sought to stop the burials, claiming they threatened health and property values. The newspaper’s report records a dispute in the cemetery’s first weeks; it does not establish the date of the first burial.

The court temporarily enjoined further burials while the complaint was heard. South-View’s organizers continued pursuing a state charter, which was approved on April 21. The conflict shows how the Black community’s effort to secure a dignified burial ground immediately met resistance from a nearby white landowner.

1904-03-31.title: Harriet Graham’s death prompts a reopened coroner’s inquiry
paragraphs: Harriet Graham, widow of South-View founder George Graham, was found dead at her Fraser Street home on March 31, 1904. A coroner’s jury initially attributed her death to heart disease. Then investigators learned that an anonymous miniature coffin containing a threatening message had been left at her door before she died.

The threat and Graham’s inheritance of property and cemetery shares prompted authorities to reopen the inquiry. The surviving account does not establish who sent the coffin or prove that Graham was murdered. Her death remains a suspicious episode in South-View’s early history, not a solved homicide.

1904-04-03.title: Harriet Graham is buried at South-View
paragraphs: Harriet Graham was buried at South-View on Easter Sunday, April 3, 1904, three days after her death. She was the widow of George Graham, one of the cemetery’s founders, and had held shares in the association herself.

Her funeral followed a coroner’s inquiry that had been reopened after a threatening miniature coffin was reported at her home. The initial finding was heart disease; suspicion lingered, but no evidence in the surviving account identified a killer or proved murder. The burial took place while those questions remained unresolved.

1968-04-04.title: Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated in Memphis
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. was shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis on April 4, 1968. He had returned to support the city’s Black sanitation workers, whose strike protested low wages, unsafe work, and the indignity of having to carry their own trash in leaking containers. King was pronounced dead at St. Joseph’s Hospital that evening.

The strike campaign showed how King’s civil-rights work had broadened into a fight over economic justice and labor. Coretta Scott King and other leaders marched with the sanitation workers on April 8. After funeral services in Atlanta the next day, King was buried at South-View; his body was moved to the King Center grounds in 1970.

1945-04-13.title: Graham Jackson plays as Roosevelt’s body leaves Warm Springs
paragraphs: On April 13, 1945, Graham Jackson played “Goin’ Home” on accordion as Franklin D. Roosevelt’s body was carried from the Little White House toward the train at Warm Springs. Jackson had performed for Roosevelt many times, and his playing turned the departure into a personal farewell as well as a public ceremony.

Life photographer Ed Clark captured Jackson in tears beside the procession. The image traveled nationally and became one of the best-known photographs of Roosevelt’s death. It records the president’s departure from Georgia; the funeral service followed in Washington and burial at Hyde Park, New York.

1886-04-21.title: Georgia grants South-View its charter after a burial dispute
paragraphs: Georgia approved the South-View Cemetery Association’s charter on April 21, 1886. Six Black Atlanta businessmen had applied to create a cemetery association and acquire land for burial. Among them was Robert Grant, a blacksmith and drayman who had helped establish Zion Hill Baptist Church and later served as its founding pastor.

The charter came after a neighboring landowner challenged burials already taking place on the grounds. It gave the organizers a legal structure for the cemetery they were building in response to segregation and unequal treatment at Atlanta burial grounds. South-View grew from the original tract into a lasting Black-owned institution.

1900-05-06.title: Henry Rutherford Butler calls for care of South-View’s grounds
paragraphs: On May 6, 1900, physician and civic leader Henry Rutherford Butler used his Atlanta Constitution column to urge South-View lot owners to keep their family plots maintained. The appeal asked readers to make the grounds “green and clean,” turning grave care into a shared responsibility for the cemetery’s future.

Butler was a prominent Black physician in Atlanta and one of the founders of the National Medical Association, created in 1895 after Black doctors were excluded from the American Medical Association. His call linked upkeep of a community cemetery with the collective institutions Black Atlantans were building under segregation.

1902-05-17.title: The 1902 Pittsburgh siege and mob violence
paragraphs: On May 17, 1902, a confrontation between Will Richardson, a Black Pittsburgh resident, and Samuel Kerlin, a white former Atlanta police officer, escalated into an armed siege. Richardson retreated to his store and residence on Amy Street, where he exchanged gunfire with police as a crowd gathered. The fighting continued into the next day; three policemen, another white man, and two Black men, including Richardson, were killed. A white mob threatened to burn the neighborhood, and fire destroyed a block of Amy Street.

Pittsburgh was an African American working-class neighborhood built around railroad jobs, homes, churches, and Black-owned businesses. The violence unfolded as Georgia’s Jim Crow laws tightened and racial hostility intensified. South-View’s burial records and cemetery history connect the event to the lives lost there; the contemporary toll and names differ among sources, so the better-established account is more useful than a single inflated casualty count.

1940-05-17.title: Henry Ossian Flipper is buried at South-View
paragraphs: Henry Ossian Flipper was buried at South-View on May 17, 1940, after dying in Atlanta at his brother Joseph’s home. Born enslaved in Thomasville, he became the first African American to graduate from West Point, in 1877, and served as an officer with the 10th Cavalry. At Fort Sill he designed a drainage system that reduced the stagnant water blamed for malaria.

The Army dismissed Flipper after an 1881 court-martial acquitted him of embezzlement but convicted him of conduct unbecoming an officer. He spent the rest of his life as an engineer, surveyor, and writer while seeking to clear his name. The Army granted him an honorable discharge in 1976; his remains were moved to Thomasville in 1978, and President Bill Clinton pardoned him in 1999.

1915-05-19.title: Atlanta buries AME bishop Henry McNeal Turner
paragraphs: Henry McNeal Turner’s body arrived in Atlanta after he died in Windsor, Ontario, while traveling on church business. On May 19, 1915, Big Bethel AME Church filled for his funeral, and a procession carried him to South-View. Turner had spent decades building AME congregations in Georgia; he had also served as a Union Army chaplain and, during Reconstruction, as one of Georgia’s Black legislators.

Turner’s public life had included both political office and religious leadership. White legislators expelled him and other Black lawmakers in 1868; in 1880 he was elected an AME bishop. He later organized missions in Africa and argued for Black emigration in response to white supremacy. A contemporary biography records that thousands viewed his body and that ministers kept a guard of honor until the burial.

1888-05-22.title: South-View’s founders transfer 25 acres to the association
paragraphs: On May 22, 1888, five South-View founders transferred about twenty-five acres to the cemetery association for $1,250. J. C. Huggins signed on behalf of Charles Morgan’s estate; Jacob McKinley, George W. Graham, Robert Grant, and Albert Watts joined the transaction. The sale put the cemetery’s original grounds under the association’s ownership and gave the new institution a formal basis for managing and expanding the burial ground.

The association had been chartered in 1886 by Black Atlantans who wanted a cemetery where their families could bury their dead with dignity. The 1888 transfer was a practical step in turning that community effort into a durable institution: a tract of land, held by an organization formed to serve Black Atlanta.

1963-06-12.title: Prince Hall Masons dedicate John Wesley Dobbs’s broken-column memorial
paragraphs: On June 12, 1963, Georgia Prince Hall Masons and Eastern Stars gathered at John Wesley Dobbs’s South-View grave to dedicate a broken-column monument. The column marked the death of a grand master and symbolized unfinished work. The ritual was led by Rev. Xenophon Lamar Neal, Dobbs’s successor; the monument was made by Turner Memorial Enterprises, a Black-owned Atlanta monument company.

Dobbs had led Georgia’s Prince Hall Grand Lodge from 1932 until his death in 1961. He also organized the Atlanta Civic and Political League and helped establish the Atlanta Negro Voters League with A. T. Walden. The memorial joined the Masonic institution he led with his campaign to make Black voter registration a source of political power in Atlanta.

1992-06-17.title: Grace Towns Hamilton dies after a career in Georgia politics
paragraphs: Grace Towns Hamilton died on June 17, 1992, after a career that moved from civil-rights administration into state politics. As executive director of the Atlanta Urban League from 1943 to 1961, she worked on housing, education, health services, and voter registration for Black residents. Her approach sought concrete gains within segregation, a strategy that eventually brought her into conflict with the national Urban League.

Hamilton won a special election in 1965 and became the first Black woman in Georgia’s General Assembly. In the House she helped write Atlanta’s 1973 city charter and took part in contentious fights over legislative districts and Black representation. She lost reelection in 1984 and later advised the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights.

1858-06-26.title: Alonzo Herndon is born enslaved in Walton County
paragraphs: Alonzo Franklin Herndon was born enslaved in Walton County, Georgia, on June 26, 1858. His mother, Sophenie, was enslaved by Frank Herndon, his white father. After emancipation, the family was forced off the farm and struggled to survive. As a young man Alonzo labored and peddled goods, then left home with eleven dollars saved and learned the barber’s trade.

Herndon opened a shop in Jonesboro and reached Atlanta in 1883. His three barbershops served elite white customers, and he invested the proceeds in real estate. In 1905 he bought a small mutual-aid association and built it into Atlanta Mutual, reorganized as Atlanta Life Insurance Company in 1922. Born with no legal claim to his father’s wealth, he became one of Atlanta’s leading Black business owners and supported schools, churches, and civic organizations.

1933-07-01.title: Jean Childs Young is born in Marion, Alabama
paragraphs: Jean Childs was born in Marion, Alabama, on July 1, 1933, the youngest of five children. She wanted to study law but found narrow options for Black women and chose teaching. At Manchester College in Indiana, she became the first African American elected May Queen in 1953 and graduated in elementary education the following year.

Young taught in Georgia and Connecticut, trained teachers for low-income schools, and worked on literacy and citizenship education. She helped develop citizenship-school curriculum for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and participated in voting-rights demonstrations. President Jimmy Carter appointed her to chair the U.S. effort for the 1979 International Year of the Child, a role that broadened her work from classrooms to children’s rights internationally.

1983-07-06.title: Atlanta honors poet, painter, and minister Thomas Jefferson Flanagan
paragraphs: Atlanta City Council proclaimed July 6, 1983, Dr. Thomas Jefferson Flanagan Day. By then Flanagan had spent decades writing for the city’s Black press: he worked with the Atlanta Independent and joined the Atlanta Daily World’s editorial staff soon after the paper began publication in 1928. His work included editorials, poetry, and books such as The Road to Mount McKeithan and The Canyons at Providence.

Flanagan also worked for the U.S. Railway Mail Service for thirty-three years, painted as a self-taught artist, and later served as an AME minister. His paintings were exhibited in the United States and Europe. He died in July 1983 at ninety-three; his funeral took place at Flipper Temple AME Church and he was buried at South-View.

2020-07-17.title: John Lewis dies after a life in the civil-rights movement and Congress
paragraphs: John Lewis died in Atlanta on July 17, 2020, after living with pancreatic cancer. As a young organizer, he joined Nashville’s sit-ins and the Freedom Rides, chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and was beaten by state troopers during the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery march. He had been one of the principal speakers at the 1963 March on Washington, where he called for federal civil-rights legislation and continued nonviolent protest.

Lewis brought the movement’s demand for voting rights into public office. He served on Atlanta’s city council before representing Georgia’s Fifth District in Congress from 1987 until his death. A long-time advocate for a national museum of African American history, he lay in state in the Capitol Rotunda before his funeral and burial at South-View.

1927-07-21.title: Alonzo Herndon dies, leaving Atlanta Life to the next generation
paragraphs: Alonzo Herndon died in Atlanta on July 21, 1927, a few weeks after his sixty-ninth birthday. Born enslaved, he had built a business spanning barbering, real estate, and insurance. In 1905 he bought a struggling mutual-aid association; by 1922 it had become Atlanta Life Insurance Company, one of a small number of Black-owned insurers to achieve legal-reserve status and expand across the South.

Herndon also gave money and leadership to Atlanta University, the YMCA, orphanages, churches, and South-View Cemetery Association. His son Norris succeeded him as Atlanta Life’s president, while his widow Jessie remained a major owner and officer. The company’s survival after Herndon’s death carried forward a business he had built into a source of Black employment, insurance, and capital.

1887-07-26.title: Mount Olivet pastor William R. Clemmons dies from gunshot injuries
paragraphs: William R. Clemmons, pastor of Atlanta’s Mount Olivet Baptist Church, died on July 26, 1887, six days after being shot in the leg on his way home from prayer meeting. Three men confronted him; after he escaped into a church member’s home, the wound worsened and an amputation failed to save him. The attackers and motive were never established.

The church bell tolled at three in the morning, drawing hundreds to Clemmons’s home. His funeral at Mount Olivet was so crowded that the floor began to buckle and the service had to move outside. A procession led by Moses Bentley’s militia company continued to South-View, where the burial rites were completed. Arrests and a $200 reward did not solve the killing.

1940-08-01.title: Benjamin E. Mays begins his Morehouse presidency
paragraphs: Morehouse College appointed Benjamin E. Mays president on August 1, 1940. The son of parents who had been enslaved in South Carolina, Mays had studied at Bates College and the University of Chicago, become a Baptist minister, and led Howard University’s School of Religion. He would remain at Morehouse for twenty-seven years, shaping the college during a period when Black institutions carried much of the burden of higher education under segregation.

Mays made chapel a regular forum for connecting faith, study, and public responsibility. Martin Luther King Jr. entered Morehouse in 1944 and often visited Mays to discuss theology and current events. Mays supported the Montgomery bus boycott and, after leaving Morehouse in 1967, became the first Black president of Atlanta’s Board of Education.

1893-08-07.title: South-View trustees ask Atlanta to waive a cemetery license fee
paragraphs: During the financial panic of 1893, South-View’s trustees asked Atlanta’s city council to waive the cemetery’s $100 license fee. They argued that many people buried there were poor and that pauper burials brought the cemetery little income. The request shows the pressure on a Black-controlled burial ground to provide low-cost funerals while meeting city expenses during a national economic crisis.

The financial disparity continued after the panic. By 1900, South-View was burying Atlanta’s Black paupers for $1.35 each, while the city paid $2 for white pauper burials at Westview. When South-View later sought the same rate, the dispute put a price on the unequal cost of caring for Atlanta’s poorest residents.

1963-08-28.title: John Lewis calls for federal action at the March on Washington
paragraphs: On August 28, 1963, twenty-three-year-old John Lewis addressed the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom as chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. He represented a younger generation facing arrests and violence in sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and voter-registration campaigns. His prepared remarks demanded effective federal civil-rights legislation and proposed a continuing campaign of nonviolent protest across the South.

Lewis spoke from the Lincoln Memorial beside labor, religious, and civil-rights leaders in a coalition of more than 200,000 people. He was the youngest principal speaker. Organizers negotiated changes to his draft before the march, but his address still pressed the national audience to move beyond promises and act against Jim Crow.

1961-08-30.title: John Wesley Dobbs dies as Atlanta schools desegregate
paragraphs: John Wesley Dobbs died on August 30, 1961, as Atlanta’s public schools began admitting their first Black students. A railway mail clerk for thirty-two years, he also led Georgia’s Prince Hall Masons and organized civic groups that pressed for Black political influence. In 1946 he and attorney A. T. Walden helped form the Atlanta Negro Voters League, coordinating voter registration and political action.

Dobbs had encouraged Martin Luther King Jr. from his youth and later testified in King’s defense after a 1960 sit-in arrest. At Dobbs’s funeral at Big Bethel AME Church on September 2, King delivered the invocation, thanking God for the life Dobbs had given Atlanta, Georgia, and the nation.

1994-09-16.title: Jean Childs Young dies after decades of education and children’s advocacy
paragraphs: Jean Childs Young died of cancer in Atlanta on September 16, 1994. She had taught elementary school, prepared teachers for low-income communities, and worked on literacy and citizenship education. During the civil-rights movement she joined demonstrations and helped develop lessons for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference’s citizenship schools, which prepared adults to participate in civic life.

President Jimmy Carter appointed Young to chair the U.S. effort for the 1979 International Year of the Child. During Andrew Young’s mayoralty, she chaired Atlanta’s Mayor’s Task Force on Public Education and helped establish programs including Dream Jamboree, a college fair for teenagers. In 1995, Southwest High School was renamed the Jean Childs Young Middle School.

1980-09-26.title: The Brown family angel falls on the day Virginia Berry dies
paragraphs: Virginia Brown Akridge Berry was an Atlanta art teacher educated at Spelman, Columbia University, and Atlanta University. She placed a stone angel on the Brown family lot at South-View. On September 26, 1980, cemetery historian Albert H. Watts recalled, the angel fell from its pedestal around noon, breaking its head and wrist. Berry died at home that evening.

The timing became a cemetery story, but no cause connected the statue’s fall with Berry’s death. The monument was repaired and returned to its pedestal. The episode survives through Watts’s recollection, as recorded by cemetery historian D. L. Henderson; no independent report of the fall was located.

1967-10-07.title: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson dies after building SNCC’s field operations
paragraphs: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson died of cancer on October 7, 1967, at twenty-five. A Spelman student, she joined Atlanta’s sit-ins, served thirty days in jail during the 1961 Rock Hill campaign, and was imprisoned for forty-five days at Mississippi’s Parchman Penitentiary after a Freedom Ride. These arrests did not push her out of the movement; she returned to the work of organizing it.

Robinson became one of SNCC’s indispensable administrators. She coordinated field staff and kept the organization’s Atlanta headquarters running while campaigns spread through the South. In 1966 she became SNCC’s executive secretary, succeeding James Forman. Her death ended a career that had helped give a decentralized movement the practical support its organizers needed.

1905-10-10.title: Amos Rucker dies after a life shaped by enslavement and Confederate memory
paragraphs: Amos Rucker died in Atlanta on October 10, 1905, at about eighty-one; his burial followed two days later. Enslaved by the Rucker family, he accompanied a young white man into Confederate service and performed the work of an army servant. After emancipation, he worked in Atlanta and became a familiar member of the W. H. T. Walker Confederate veterans’ camp, where he could recite the old company roll from memory. A 1898 account’s own language describes the relationship as one between master and slave, even as it praised Rucker’s loyalty.

Rucker’s former comrades gave him a Confederate-style funeral, with a gray uniform, flag, veterans as pallbearers, and former Confederate general Clement A. Evans conducting the service. Supporters urged Georgia to recognize his wartime service, but the sources located here document a campaign for recognition, not enlistment or a verified medal. His public image as a Confederate veteran was built after the war around a man who had been enslaved and forced into service.

1905-10-12.title: Amos Rucker dies and is buried at South-View
paragraphs: Amos Rucker died in Atlanta on October 10, 1905, at about eighty-one, and was buried at South-View two days later. Enslaved by the Rucker family, he was forced to accompany a young white man into Confederate service, where he worked as an army servant. After emancipation he worked in Atlanta’s post office and became a familiar member of the W. H. T. Walker veterans’ camp.

Former governor Allen D. Candler and Confederate veterans joined Rucker’s funeral; former Confederate general Clement A. Evans conducted the service. Veterans dressed him in a gray uniform and placed a Confederate flag over his coffin. The honors show how white veterans folded a formerly enslaved man into Confederate remembrance, often describing coerced service as loyalty. The record supports his role as an army servant, not an enlisted soldier or verified medal recipient.

1944-10-13.title: Walter Drake Westmoreland is shot down over Hungary
paragraphs: First Lieutenant Walter Drake Westmoreland was killed on October 13, 1944, when German antiaircraft fire struck his P-51 near Lake Balaton, Hungary. He was returning from an escort mission to the Blechhammer oil refinery. Westmoreland, an Atlanta native, flew with the 302nd Fighter Squadron of the 332nd Fighter Group; the Air Force record identifies his Mustang as Dopey.

The 332nd was one of the Army Air Forces’ segregated Black fighter groups, known for escorting American bombers across Europe. Its pilots fought Nazi forces abroad while confronting discrimination in the military at home. Westmoreland’s remains were eventually returned to Atlanta and he was buried at South-View.

1964-10-14.title: Coretta Scott King brings Martin Luther King Jr. news of the Nobel Prize
paragraphs: On October 14, 1964, Coretta Scott King telephoned her husband in an Atlanta hospital with news that he had been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. At thirty-five, Martin Luther King Jr. was the youngest man to receive the award at that time. The Nobel Committee recognized his leadership in the nonviolent campaign against racial injustice.

The announcement followed the Montgomery bus boycott, the Birmingham campaign and the March on Washington, but came while organizers still faced violence and barriers to voting. King said the honor belonged to the wider movement, and he later shared the prize money among civil-rights organizations. He traveled to Oslo to receive it in December.

1895-10-21.title: John W. E. Bowen calls for education and opportunity at Atlanta’s exposition
paragraphs: On October 21, 1895, theologian John Wesley Edward Bowen delivered “An Appeal to the King” during Negro Day at Atlanta’s Cotton States and International Exposition. He praised Black Americans’ achievements since emancipation and pressed for education and fuller opportunity. His address spoke to the limits imposed on Black life even as the exposition presented itself as a showcase of regional progress.

Bowen was a professor at Gammon Theological Seminary and had earned a doctorate from Boston University in 1887. He later became Gammon’s president and co-founded the Voice of the Negro. During Atlanta’s 1906 racial massacre, he sheltered Black residents at the seminary despite being beaten and arrested.

1885-10-26.title: Sterling Watts is buried in Westview’s segregated Rest Haven section
paragraphs: Sterling Watts was buried in Rest Haven, the section of Atlanta’s Westview Cemetery set aside for African Americans, on October 26, 1885. His son Albert Watts was among the Black Atlantans who soon organized a cemetery under Black community ownership. South-View’s founders sought a place where Black families could make decisions about burial and care themselves.

The burial is part of the origin story of South-View, founded the following year by Black Atlanta businessmen and community leaders. Accounts describing exactly what Albert witnessed or thought at his father’s funeral are later reconstructions; the documented point is that segregation and poor conditions at Rest Haven helped spur the new cemetery.

1904-11-08.title: Horace Mann Bond is born in Nashville
paragraphs: Horace Mann Bond was born in Nashville, Tennessee, on November 8, 1904, into a family of educators and ministers. He entered Lincoln University at fourteen, graduated in 1923 and earned a doctorate at the University of Chicago. His scholarship examined how poverty and unequal schools shaped Black children’s educational opportunities.

Bond led Fort Valley State College from 1939 to 1945, expanding its resources and strengthening its curriculum, then became Lincoln University’s first Black president. In 1953 he joined historians John Hope Franklin and C. Vann Woodward in research for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund that contributed to the arguments in Brown v. Board of Education.

1898-11-09.title: Nineteen-year-old Wade Hampton is executed at Atlanta’s Tower jail
paragraphs: Wade Hampton was nineteen when he was hanged at Atlanta’s new Fulton County jail, known as the Tower, on November 9, 1898. He had first been imprisoned as a child for burglary and leased to work at the Chattahoochee Brick Company; an explosion there cost him a leg. He was later convicted of killing another young prisoner and sentenced to death.

Hampton asked to hear the Methodist hymn “Am I Born to Die?” before the execution. The account of his final hours records that the drop failed to break his neck and he died by strangulation. His life shows how Georgia’s convict-leasing system subjected children as well as adults to forced labor and physical danger.

1898-11-10.title: Wade Hampton is buried at South-View after his execution
paragraphs: Wade Hampton was buried at South-View on November 10, 1898, the day after he was executed at Fulton County’s Tower jail. Undertaker L. L. Lee removed the body from the jail. Hampton was nineteen.

As a child, Hampton had been imprisoned for burglary and sent to labor at the Chattahoochee Brick Company under Georgia’s convict-lease system, where an explosion cost him a leg. In 1898 he was executed after being convicted of killing another prisoner. His burial followed a life shaped by a system that made Black people’s labor and bodies subject to private control.

1927-11-17.title: A young descendant unveils Bishop Lucius Holsey’s monument
paragraphs: On November 17, 1927, a five-year-old great-granddaughter unveiled a marble monument to Bishop Lucius Henry Holsey at South-View. About five hundred people attended, many arriving by special streetcars and buses. Black Methodist congregations had raised funds for the memorial, which honored Holsey as a bishop, preacher and orator.

Born enslaved in 1842, Holsey helped build the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church after emancipation and was elected a bishop in 1873. He also campaigned for Black education: his appeal to white southern Methodists helped establish Paine College in Augusta. The South-View gathering brought church members together to remember a leader whose work joined religious institution-building with education.

1955-12-05.title: Montgomery’s Black residents begin a bus boycott and form the MIA
paragraphs: On December 5, 1955, about 90 percent of Montgomery’s Black residents stayed off the buses after Rosa Parks’s arrest four days earlier. Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council had printed and distributed leaflets calling for the one-day protest. That afternoon, local ministers and organizers formed the Montgomery Improvement Association and elected the young Dexter Avenue Baptist Church pastor Martin Luther King Jr. as president.

At a mass meeting that evening, thousands voted to continue the boycott. Residents kept it going for more than a year by walking, sharing rides and organizing a community carpool despite arrests, threats and bombings. A federal court challenge, Browder v. Gayle, struck down bus segregation; the boycott ended in December 1956 after the ruling took effect.

1886-12-06.title: Charles H. Morgan buys the first recorded South-View shares
paragraphs: On December 6, 1886, South-View Cemetery Association’s stock book recorded Charles H. Morgan buying its first three shares. A grocer and one of the men who petitioned for the cemetery’s charter, Morgan committed money to a new Black-led institution only months after its founding. Each share was valued at one hundred dollars.

Morgan’s investment came in the cemetery’s first year of operation, when Black Atlantans were building an organization that could provide burial on terms they controlled. He died less than two weeks later and was buried in a family lot at South-View on December 17.

1964-12-10.title: Martin Luther King Jr. accepts the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. accepted the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo on December 10, 1964. He dedicated it to the civil-rights movement and the people risking their safety to challenge segregation. In his speech, he recalled the violence directed at Black children in Birmingham and at voting-rights workers in Mississippi, insisting that the struggle was still unfinished.

King described nonviolent protest as an active force for social change and framed the award as a trust held on behalf of the movement. At thirty-five, he was the youngest Nobel Peace laureate at the time. He shared the prize money with civil-rights organizations.

1886-12-17.title: South-View co-founder Charles H. Morgan is buried
paragraphs: Charles H. Morgan was buried at South-View on December 17, 1886, eleven days after the cemetery’s stock book recorded his purchase of three shares. Morgan was a grocer, property owner and charter petitioner for the new cemetery. His family lot became one of the early burial places at the institution he had helped establish.

Morgan’s death came while the association was still organizing its land, lots and finances. His son-in-law John C. Huggins later took part in the cemetery’s continuing growth, reflecting how families of the founders helped sustain South-View across generations.

1972-12-21.title: Educator and scholar Horace Mann Bond dies
paragraphs: Horace Mann Bond died on December 21, 1972, after retiring the previous year from Atlanta University. He had led Fort Valley State College and Lincoln University, then returned to Atlanta as a dean and education researcher. At each institution he worked to strengthen Black higher education while studying the barriers segregation placed before Black students.

In 1953 Bond joined historians John Hope Franklin and C. Vann Woodward in research for the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. Their work contributed to the evidence and arguments presented in Brown v. Board of Education. Bond’s research connected the conditions Black children experienced in schools to the constitutional challenge to segregation.

1994-12-23.title: Librarian Annie L. McPheeters dies after building Atlanta’s Black history collection
paragraphs: Annie L. McPheeters died on December 23, 1994, at eighty-six, months after the Auburn Avenue Research Library opened in Atlanta. She had joined the Auburn Branch as an assistant librarian in 1934 and developed its Negro History Collection, bringing together books and resources about people of African descent. That collection became a foundation for the research library that opened decades later.

McPheeters helped expand library service for Black Atlantans and worked with advocates who won desegregation of the city’s public libraries in 1959. In 1966 she became Georgia State College’s first Black reference librarian. Her career connected everyday public access to books with the preservation of Black history for future researchers.

1885-12-26.title: Atlanta educator Bazoline E. Usher is born
paragraphs: Bazoline Estelle Usher was born in Walton County, Georgia, on December 26, 1885. She studied at Atlanta University and graduated in 1906, then taught in Virginia before returning to Atlanta in 1915. Over the next decades she became a teacher, principal and leader in the city’s public education system.

Usher supervised Atlanta’s African American schools and helped expand their facilities, including the opening of seven elementary schools. In 1943 she also helped organize Girl Scout troops for Black girls, creating space for leadership and outdoor activities in a segregated city. Her work joined the struggle for quality Black education with opportunities for girls beyond the classroom.

2012-12-31.title: Lillian Miles Lewis dies after a career in libraries and public service
paragraphs: Lillian Miles Lewis died in Atlanta on December 31, 2012, at seventy-three. A trained librarian, she worked at Atlanta University and later held leadership posts at Clark Atlanta University, including directing external affairs in its research office. She also served on Georgia’s State Ethics Commission and contributed to civic and professional organizations.

Lewis married John Lewis in 1968 and became a trusted adviser as he moved from civil-rights organizing into public office. She encouraged his 1977 congressional campaign and continued her own work in education, international affairs and community service. Her career and influence extended well beyond her public identity as the congressman’s wife.

william-h-crogman.name: William H. Crogman
paragraphs: William Henry Crogman was born in Philipsburg on the Caribbean island of Sint Maarten in 1841. After emancipation, he pursued an education in the United States, studied at Claflin University, and joined Atlanta’s Clark University in 1876 to teach Greek and Latin.

Crogman became one of Clark’s most respected scholars and served as its president from 1903 to 1910. He argued for broad liberal-arts education and equal citizenship, using classical learning to challenge the assumption that Black students should receive only narrow vocational training.

grace-towns-hamilton.name: Grace Towns Hamilton
paragraphs: Grace Towns Hamilton was born in Atlanta in 1907 and trained as an educator and social scientist. She led the Atlanta Urban League from 1943 to 1961, directing campaigns that addressed housing, health care, school inequality, and voter registration within the constraints of segregation.

Hamilton entered the Georgia House in 1966 as the first African American woman elected to the state legislature. She served until 1985, working on reapportionment and city-government reform so Black residents could gain fairer representation in public decisions.

alonzo-herndon.name: Alonzo Herndon
paragraphs: Born enslaved in 1858, Alonzo Herndon worked as a farm laborer before learning the barber trade after emancipation. In Atlanta he built a chain of barbershops, including a prominent shop on Peachtree Street that served Black professionals and became a hub of Black business life.

Herndon acquired the Atlanta Benevolent and Protective Association in 1905 and grew it into Atlanta Life Insurance Company. The insurer served Black policyholders turned away by white firms, employed Black professionals, and helped finance civic institutions; Herndon became one of Atlanta’s leading Black businessmen and philanthropists.

annie-l-mcpheeters.name: Annie L. McPheeters
paragraphs: Annie Lou McPheeters trained as a librarian at Hampton and Columbia and began working in Atlanta’s segregated public library system in the 1930s. At Auburn Branch she developed the Negro History Collection and created programs that helped Black readers study history, literature, and public affairs.

McPheeters expanded library service despite separate facilities and unequal resources. She advocated for desegregation, later became the first Black faculty member at Georgia State University, and left papers that preserve the work of Black librarians and readers in Atlanta.

graham-w-jackson-sr.name: Graham W. Jackson Sr.
paragraphs: Graham Washington Jackson Sr. was an Atlanta musician, bandleader, and teacher known for his command of organ, piano, and accordion. He performed with his group the Seminole Syncopators and taught at Booker T. Washington High School, helping shape the city’s Black music scene during segregation.

Jackson became a nationally recognized figure through his friendship with Franklin D. Roosevelt. After Roosevelt died in Warm Springs in 1945, Jackson played “Goin’ Home” on accordion beside the departing funeral train; the photograph of his tears became an image of both personal grief and public mourning.

ludie-clay-andrews.name: Ludie Clay Andrews
paragraphs: Ludie Clay Andrews trained as a nurse at Spelman’s MacVicar Hospital program, graduating in 1906, and became a leader in Georgia’s Black nursing schools. She supervised training programs at Lula Grove Hospital and Grady Hospital and helped prepare generations of nurses to serve Black communities.

Georgia barred Black nurses from its licensing examination, so Andrews spent years challenging the policy and refused an individual exception that would not help other nurses. The state opened registration to qualified Black nurses around 1919–1920, and Andrews became Georgia’s first Black registered nurse.

john-lewis.name: John Lewis
paragraphs: John Lewis grew up on his family’s farm in Alabama and was inspired by the Montgomery bus boycott to join the freedom struggle. A student at Fisk University, he helped found SNCC, became its chairman, took part in the Freedom Rides, and was the youngest speaker at the 1963 March on Washington.

Lewis endured arrests and violence while organizing for voting rights, most famously when troopers beat him on Selma’s Edmund Pettus Bridge on Bloody Sunday in 1965. He later served Atlanta in Congress for 33 years, carrying the movement’s push for equal political participation into national government.

paragraphs: Dinah Watts Pace was born enslaved in Georgia in 1853 and later studied at Atlanta University, graduating from its normal department in 1883. She went to Covington to teach, but soon made education and child welfare her life’s work.

Pace founded a school and home for Black children, taking in orphans and educating hundreds over more than forty years. Her institution filled urgent needs in a segregated society where public support was limited; local residents remembered her as a community builder as well as a teacher.

freddye-henderson.name: Freddye Henderson
paragraphs: Freddye Scarborough Henderson was an Atlanta educator, columnist, entrepreneur, and advocate for international travel. In 1955 she and her husband, James, founded Henderson Travel Service, a Black-owned agency that arranged trips for clients who often faced discrimination from mainstream travel companies.

The agency helped African Americans travel abroad during the Jim Crow era, including a 1957 group journey to Ghana for its independence celebrations. Henderson’s work connected business ownership with a wider vision of cultural exchange and mobility for Black travelers.

martin-luther-king-jr.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. grew up in Atlanta’s Ebenezer Baptist Church and became a Baptist minister shaped by the Black church, Gandhian nonviolence, and the struggle against segregation. The Montgomery bus boycott made him a national leader, and he later helped build the Southern Christian Leadership Conference to coordinate campaigns across the South.

King’s public work joined desegregation to voting rights, labor, and economic justice. From Birmingham and Selma to Memphis, he urged nonviolent direct action against systems that denied Black Americans equal citizenship; he was assassinated while supporting Memphis sanitation workers in 1968.

benjamin-e-mays.name: Benjamin E. Mays
paragraphs: Benjamin Elijah Mays was born in South Carolina in 1894 to parents who had been enslaved. He studied at Bates College and the University of Chicago, became a Baptist minister and scholar, and served as dean of Howard University’s School of Religion before returning to Atlanta.

As president of Morehouse College from 1940 to 1967, Mays built the school’s academic reputation and urged students to confront injustice. Martin Luther King Jr. later called him his spiritual mentor. After retiring, Mays chaired Atlanta’s school board during desegregation; he was first buried at South-View before reinterment at Morehouse.

jean-childs-young.name: Jean Childs Young
paragraphs: Jean Childs Young was born in Marion, Alabama, in 1933 and trained as a teacher after graduating from Manchester College. She taught in Atlanta and took part in civil-rights activism, including the city’s 1961 lunch-counter campaign, the Selma voting-rights march, and the Poor People’s Campaign.

Young helped develop citizenship education for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and became a national advocate for children, serving as chair of the U.S. Committee for UNICEF. As Atlanta’s first lady during Andrew Young’s mayoral terms, she created education and career programs for local youth.

horace-mann-bond.name: Horace Mann Bond
paragraphs: Horace Mann Bond was born in Nashville in 1904 and became a sociologist, education researcher, and college administrator. After studying at Lincoln University and the University of Chicago, he led Fort Valley State College in Georgia and later Lincoln University, where he became the first Black and first alumnus president.

Bond documented the unequal resources and opportunities facing Black students and produced research used by the NAACP Legal Defense Fund in the period of Brown v. Board of Education. He wrote about Black education and Pan-Africanism and was the father of civil-rights leader Julian Bond.

Usher became Atlanta’s first Black supervisor of African American schools and the first Black official with an office at City Hall. In 1943 she organized Girl Scout troops for Black girls, opening space for leadership and outdoor activities when segregation excluded them from many programs.

lillian-miles-lewis.name: Lillian Miles Lewis
paragraphs: Lillian Miles Lewis was born in Los Angeles in 1939 and developed an international outlook through study, library work, and two years as a volunteer teacher in Nigeria. She earned a master’s degree in library science and joined Atlanta University in 1965 as a librarian and director of special collections.

Lewis continued her work in higher-education administration at Clark Atlanta University and served on Georgia’s State Ethics Commission. She married John Lewis in 1968 and was his close adviser throughout his public career; her papers preserve her own professional work as well as their shared life.

robert-grant.name: Robert Grant
paragraphs: After emancipation, Robert Grant helped build institutions that gave Atlanta’s Black community places to worship and organize. A skilled blacksmith and drayman, he joined seven members of Friendship Baptist Church in founding Zion Hill Baptist Church in 1872. As its first pastor, he organized a deacon board, a mothers’ board, a choir, and Sunday school.

Grant also invested in South-View Cemetery, one of six Black businessmen named in the cemetery association’s charter application in 1886. In a segregated city where Black families were often denied dignified burial options, the cemetery and its founding church represented community ownership and self-determination. Zion Hill’s archival history dates Grant’s pastorate to 1872–1876 and says he died in 1896; a precise birth or death day has not been established.

john-w-dobbs.name: John W. Dobbs
paragraphs: John Wesley Dobbs became one of Atlanta’s most influential Black civic organizers in the decades when Jim Crow laws restricted voting and public life. After leaving Atlanta Baptist College to support his family, he passed a civil-service exam and worked for 32 years as a railway mail clerk. He kept studying on his own and became known around Auburn Avenue as “the Grand” for his leadership in Prince Hall Freemasonry.

Dobbs turned that standing into political organizing. He founded the Atlanta Civic and Political League in 1936 and co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League with attorney A. T. Walden in 1946. Their registration drives helped build pressure for Atlanta’s first eight Black police officers in 1948 and streetlights on Auburn Avenue the next year. Dobbs helped popularize “Sweet Auburn,” a name for the Black business and civic district.

moses-amos.name: Dr. Moses Amos
paragraphs: Moses Amos learned pharmacy as an apprentice in Atlanta under druggist J. C. Huss. In the early twentieth century, he became Georgia’s first licensed Black pharmacist, at a time when segregated health care and discrimination limited Black residents’ access to medicines and professional training. He went on to acquire the Auburn Avenue drugstore where he had worked and, in 1914, reopened it as Gate City Drug Store.

Gate City was more than a shop: it served a growing Black neighborhood and became part of Sweet Auburn’s network of Black-owned businesses. Amos hired Black women as clerks, mentored younger pharmacists, and helped make pharmacy a path into health care and entrepreneurship. The business later moved to the West Side under Amos and his nephew, Miles Green Amos.

carolyn-d-yancey.name: Carolyn D. Yancey
paragraphs: Carolyn Dunbar Yancey began her career as a teacher after studying education and social work. Born in Detroit in 1921, she later moved with her family to Atlanta, where she became active in civic organizations and public education. In 1982, voters elected her to the Atlanta Board of Education, where she served for sixteen years.

In 1985, Governor Joe Frank Harris appointed Yancey to the University System of Georgia Board of Regents, making her the first Black woman to serve on that board. Her work placed her in institutions that shaped both public schools and higher education during a period of change in Atlanta. She died in 2010.

geneva-haugabrooks.name: Geneva Haugabrooks
paragraphs: Geneva Moton Haugabrooks turned a small start into a long-running business on Auburn Avenue. After studying at Spelman and working as a teacher, she opened Haugabrooks Funeral Home in 1929 with roughly $300. She became one of Atlanta’s pioneering Black women funeral directors and a familiar figure in the city’s African American community, often called “Ma Haugabrooks.”

The funeral home met a vital need in a segregated city, providing funeral services and helping families honor their dead. Haugabrooks also supported civic, religious, and charitable groups, including Wheat Street Baptist Church, the Urban League, and voter-registration efforts. Her business became a neighborhood institution and remained part of Sweet Auburn’s Black-owned commercial life for decades.

john-w-e-bowen.name: John W. E. Bowen
paragraphs: John Wesley Edward Bowen was a theologian, minister, and educator whose scholarship challenged the racial assumptions of his era. Born in New Orleans in 1855, he studied at New Orleans University and Boston University, where he became one of the first African Americans to earn a Ph.D. He taught at Morgan College and Howard University before joining Gammon Theological Seminary in Atlanta in 1893 as its first full-time Black professor.

Bowen later led Gammon as president and helped train generations of Black clergy. At the 1895 Cotton States and International Exposition, he delivered “An Appeal to the King,” a public argument for Black citizenship and equality. During Atlanta’s 1906 racial violence, Bowen opened Gammon’s campus as a refuge and was himself beaten and arrested. He also edited The Voice of the Negro and wrote on religion, education, and African American life.
